title: Listening in Todi
hookLine: a short Todi hymn that speaks to a mother: the Guru's feet are sweet

lines: GUESS WHAT, GUESS WHO I MET.
ONE SHORT HYMN, LINE BY LINE.
cards: Maaee. Mother. A word called from the next room, or down the stairs, or into a phone.
When something good happens, there can be one person you want to tell before anyone else: guess what, guess who I met. Today, slow right down and listen to one short hymn in Todi, word by word.
It's by Guru Arjan, and it begins exactly like that: a voice turning to its mother to share something sweet. Today: listening in Todi.

teach.b: The heading says Todi, mahala five: Guru Arjan. Its refrain, the rahao, is the heart of it.
Say the words slowly: maaee charan gur meethe. Maaee: mother, the way you'd call to her from the next room. Charan: feet.

teach.h: MOTHER, THE GURU'S FEET ARE SWEET.
teach.b: Mother, the Guru's feet are sweet. Feet may sound like an odd thing to call sweet.

But in the Granth the Guru's feet are a picture of humility and closeness: you sit low, near the one you love, close enough to touch the dust they walk in. Calling them sweet is the language of affection, not of ceremony.
The refrain goes on, in paraphrase: by great good fortune the Lord grants this, and the sight of the Guru brings fruit beyond counting.

teach.h: A CONFIDENCE SHARED WITH A MOTHER.
teach.b: So it's shaped like a confidence: good news about the Guru, told to a mother, the way good news gets shared at a kitchen counter.
Spoken to someone close, about someone loved, in the plainest speech there is: tender words. Yesterday's hymn said, without the Lord, my mind cannot live. Today's says, mother, it's sweet.
Need, and then the sweetness of having it met.

how: Guru Arjan's Todi hymns, including maaee charan gur meethe, are sung in kirtan in Raga Todi, and Sikhs reading the Granth at home or in the sangat read them with their meanings.

o: a lullaby a mother sings to her child at dawn
Guru Arjan's refrain: mother, the Guru's feet are sweet
a lament sung to a mother after someone has died

games.q: word by word — tap the pairs.

s: this Todi hymn is by Guru Arjan
the heading says Todi, mahala five.
calling the Guru's feet sweet is the language of ceremony
it's the language of affection: sitting low and close to the one you love.

games.q: the refrain carries good news about the Guru. whom does it speak to?
games.why: the refrain begins maaee, mother: the Guru's feet are sweet. good news shared with someone close.

practice: Say the four words slowly, with a breath between each, maaee, charan, gur, meethe, or listen to a recording of this hymn with the words in front of you.

Then sit in the quiet that follows and let someone come to mind you would run to with good news, living or gone, and stay with them, with Waheguru if you pray, or just letting them be close if you don't.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Todi. Guru Arjan's short hymn, maaee charan gur meethe: mother, the Guru's feet are sweet, read along slowly, word by word. Today's word.

orig.note: mother, the Guru's feet are sweet: the refrain of Guru Arjan's hymn in Todi.

carryVoice: Your line: tender words. Plain speech, to someone close, about someone loved. I'll be here tomorrow.
